Thanks, it's always better to read it from the source as opposed to an interpretation.

Thanks - as a stage 4 (currently in remission), cancer treatment seems to be still in the dark ages. Have experienced both radiation and chemotherapy. What I learned was that the most common cancer treatments are counter intuitive to any other medical procedure that I am aware.

Radiation - "the surgeon cut out all the cancer tissue he could find - now let's spray the area with doses of x-ray radiation" (I have looked but haven't found that anyone has ever developed cancer from radiation treatments....)

Chemo - "let's now pump toxic chemicals into you that hopefully will kill more cancerous cells than healthy cells...."

Don't get me wrong - am extremely grateful to be alive and on the mend but have been reading these stories about what's on the horizon for treatment and am thinking that modern medicine is finally on the right path to developing successful cures for cancer.

Doc here.

Radiation is used instead of surgery in certain tumors like prostate or lung cancer, or after surgery to kill off any remaining cancer cells. It may seem barbaric, but it's actually freaking awesome. Think about it, we can CURE your cancer without ever poking you with needles or letting a scapel touch you. Modern radiation delivery systems allow for excellent targeting of the cancer and very few side effects (rarely do we "burn" patients, and if we did so it was because that's where the cancer was!). Yes, you can get cancer from radiation, just like any Chest X-ray or CT scan. The chance is as high as 0.5% or 1 in 200 patients. If that seems high to you, realize that the chance of you dieing from your cancer because you skipped radiotherapy is always much much higher. Also, radiation induced cancer has a latency period (ie a delay) of 8-20 years, so if your'e one of the unlucky few who have a cancer from radiation, you've already been lucky enough to have survived your first cancer.

The role of chemo is to kill off currently reproducing cells. That includes cancer cells, but also cells lining the gut (nausea, diarrhea), cells making red and white blood cells (fatigue, risk of infection) and he few muscle, skin, and other cells that happen to be dividing at that time. We only say "hopefully" because all cancers are different and it really sucks to promise to a patient that the chemo will work when it sometime doesn't. Furthermore, there are A LOT of newer drugs that we call chemo but are better termed "systemic therapy" that are targeted to a specific cell marker and therefore have very limited side effects while still being highly effective (as long as you target the right cancer).

Now as to the OP, yeah of course it may cause worse QOL but also equally may stop the cancer and give months to years of survival. No one has a crystal ball and 95% of the cancer docs I have known only have the patient's best interests at heart.

BTW, so glad you're in remission! I highly encourage spending your time with as much loved ones as possible and otherwise doing some traveling. There is typically 3-6months before any recurrences, so use this time well.

Glad to hear of your remission. Having done some research in radiation oncology, I understand what you mean -- we've been using some of the same chemo drugs for decades (cisplatin comes to mind). However, the technology is definitely progressing. IMRT and proton therapy are pretty fascinating treatment methods, for instance.
It's always amazing how shitty Cancer is.

My mother is an RN in a rehab/hospice facility and time and time again she sees her end stage patients taking greedy doctors advice and spending their final days on chemo with no quality of life. There isn't a doctor she's met that wont advise chemo for a patient, even if it's clear they will succumb to the cancer. It's a real shame and she does her best to inform people about it so they can avoid it, but many choose the chemo and end up dying full of tubes in a hospital bed instead of home surrounded by family. She'll always ask the family's or patients struggling with the decision what's more important a couple more months maybe, or your last few weeks, maybe a month with your family and not in a hospital bed.

Death is a big issue that needs addressing in this country, doctors need to be able to direct people to the proper treatment for quality of life instead of always looking to extend it. My step grand father recently passed from stage 4 lung cancer (never smoked). It started there and quickly spread everywhere. The doctors gave him a positive prognosis with chemo (maybe years they said) and he took it. He was very well for a month, moving about, smiling interacting, and then boom, bedridden and dying, he spent his final week in bed unable to even open his eyes. The cancer came back far more aggressive and maybe a month and a half later, this after weeks of debilitating chemo. He never was able to communicate it, but I don't think he'd have done it the same had he known how it would end.

There is a joke about oncologists: How many does it take to carry a casket at a funeral? Seven: 6 to carry the casket and 1 to give one more round of chemo.

Like all jokes that's an exaggeration, but there is a reason for the stereotype. Some, though not all oncologists give end stage patients chemo past a point of reasonableness. However if you think that is due to greedy oncologists you are mistaken. It's really hard to tell someone that they are dying and the time when they will die is soon. I'm an ER doc so fortunately I don't have to have that talk too often, but it happens more than I would like. Generally it's because well meaning physicians faced with patients who are desperate for some hope are more willing to offer truly futile care. It's also not because doctors don't try to have those conversations - it's just that some patients have a great deal more difficulty dealing with them. Unfortunately when I end up having the talk with patients, it's often during a crisis - which makes it that much harder. Basically it just sucks all around.

Now this is a spectrum - some doctors are great at having the talk, some suck ass. As a general rule, oncologists are better at it than most - if nothing else because they have to do it more. But no one is perfect, so you are going to have futile care be delivered at patient request (and even demand). The best we can hope for is to minimize the problem.

There are three major Judo organizations in the United States. They are the USJA, USJF, and USJI (more commonly as USA Judo). For someone at your level (a beginner) which organization you join is not relevant as long as they belong to those three. You do not want to join a Judo club that belongs to a different organization like the USMAA as an up and coming Judoka. Your rank will not be recognized.
